subject: Version Control Systems

assessmentTargets.concept: Identify the three areas of a Git workflow: Working Directory, Staging Area, and Repository.
assessmentTargets.supportingEvidence: The next one you have is git add. So this is, if you remember in your git workflow, I told you we have three areas. Working directory, staging area and git repository.
assessmentTargets.evidenceSpan: Explanation of the three Git areas
assessmentTargets.instruction: List the three areas and briefly describe their role.

assessmentTargets.concept: Explain how `git add` moves changes from the Working Directory to the Staging Area, including adding all files versus a single file.
assessmentTargets.supportingEvidence: If you can simply write git add space dot, that means all the changes that you have done in your project will be saved. ... you can write git space add space a dot txt. So only the changes of that particular file will be saved into the staging area.
assessmentTargets.evidenceSpan: Demonstration of git add syntax for all files and a specific file
assessmentTargets.instruction: Describe the command syntax for adding all changes versus a single file.

assessmentTargets.concept: Describe the purpose of `git commit`, the role of a commit message, and what happens to staged changes.
assessmentTargets.supportingEvidence: Git commit will save the changes of your particular file into the repository... you have to use a command git commit. And you have to give a message.
assessmentTargets.evidenceSpan: Explanation of git commit and commit messages
assessmentTargets.instruction: Explain why a descriptive commit message is recommended.

assessmentTargets.concept: Analyze how `git diff` shows differences between the previous commit and the current working state.
assessmentTargets.supportingEvidence: The next one is git diff. ... it will compare the changes of your current file with the previous version.
assessmentTargets.instruction: Interpret a sample `git diff` output to identify added and removed lines.

assessmentTargets.subtopic: Undoing Changes (git reset vs git restore)
assessmentTargets.concept: Differentiate between `git reset` and `git restore` for reverting staged and working‑directory changes.
assessmentTargets.supportingEvidence: When I type git reset. All the changes will be reverted back... I will simply type git restore dot. When I do that ... the new line is also deleted.
assessmentTargets.evidenceSpan: Demonstration of git reset and git restore commands
assessmentTargets.instruction: Choose the appropriate command for each undo scenario and justify your choice.

reserveTargets.concept: Use `git help` to retrieve syntax and options for any Git command.
reserveTargets.supportingEvidence: Now say suppose you forgot how to use a particular command in git. Then simply write git space help space that command name.

reserveTargets.concept: Identify the installed Git version using the appropriate command.
reserveTargets.supportingEvidence: So before that let's start with knowing what is the git version. So I will simply type git space hyphen hyphen version.
reserveTargets.instruction: Run the command and note the output format.

reserveTargets.concept: Explain how `git init` converts a normal folder into a Git repository.
reserveTargets.supportingEvidence: You have to type git space init. This particular folder ... is converted into a git repository.
reserveTargets.instruction: List the files/folders created after initialization.
